🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.83% (intraday, 7-year +26bp). At trading day 14 (last close) it was -1.44% against a five-campaign average of -0.60% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. Spreads have barely moved, so this is a rates story, not credit. The 10-year is +32bp since the hike vs a +7bp campaign average at the same point.
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 702bp against a five-year average of 409bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +30bp and BB +26bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.28 → 0.50 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+0bp).
  • Stocks: US stock futures point lower after Wednesday's gain; Europe is falling harder.
  • FX: The dollar is jumping and the euro is sliding to multi-month lows.
  • Technicals: US stocks are stretched far above their long-term averages; gold sits below them.
  • Sectors: Tech and energy lead the year; banks and property lagged this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lending to the weakest junk companies is getting much costlier; stronger borrowers are calm.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; the main risks are bond yields, junk debt and war.
  • Inflation: Underlying inflation is easing slowly, but energy keeps the headline numbers sticky.
  • Tech Bubble: Prices are pricey but not 2000-crazy; credit and market calm look complacent.
  • Earnings & IPOs: JPMorgan opens bank earnings Oct 13; Delta's results carry the biggest expected swing.
  • Iran: The war is now in its eighth month; Red Sea fighting keeps oil near $100.
  • Warsh: The Fed hiked in September; deputies now say patience, so probably a pause next.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term: rising yields and a strong dollar squeeze stocks and gold.
  • Trades: Trim stretched stocks, favor the dollar, avoid the weakest junk, wait on gold.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 sell, 24 hold long, 20 stay out

Pre-market tone has flipped from Wednesday's risk-on close. The S&P 500 finished the prior session at 7818.93 (+0.578599%), the Nasdaq at 27599.89 (+0.4461135%) and the Dow at 51521.28 (+0.4942274%). Under the surface it was narrower: the Russell 2000 fell -0.5914364% and VIX rose to 15.76 from 15.01. This morning the driver is a global bond selloff. The US 10Y is at 5.3411% (+6.18bp), the 30Y at 5.7158%, the 2Y at 4.8143%, gilts are +10.1bp at 5.476% and Bunds are +3.7bp at 3.515%. ES is -0.412750825501651%, NQ -0.7106953697601105% and Dow futures -0.8028408213679172%. Europe is taking the hit: Euro Stoxx 50 -1.680264%, STOXX 600 -0.9848735%, FTSE -0.5876667%. The dollar is surging (DXY 102.49, +0.645173961289559%; EUR/USD 1.118), and gold (-1.6887%) and silver (-2.4957%) are being sold despite Brent at 101.48. The second story is in credit. Broad IG (0.8%) and HY (2.98%) spreads still look calm, but CCC stress is extreme. The Bloomberg Caa–B gap is at 702bp against a 5y average of ~409bp, in the 99.9th percentile of the last 5 years. It is the widest since 2020-04-27 and +180bp over 3 months; the FRED CCC–B cross-check is at 897bp, in the 100th percentile (computed). Is it spreading up the ladder? Partly. Over the past month single-B widened +30bp and Ba widened +26bp. However, the B–Ba gap (107bp) is still below its 5y average and IG is flat on the month at 80bp. The Caa/B correlation of daily moves has risen to 0.50 from 0.28 three months ago, which points to growing linkage, but it is still below its 0.70 5y median. Last week also brought a pullback: Caa -12bp, B -15bp, Ba -8bp. This is a description of the data, not a validated signal. Sentiment is complacent but not euphoric. Equities sit near the top of their historical range versus their moving averages, while the bond market is starting to push back.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.00 vol points (78th percentile of the 36 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 105.2 (76th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 113bp (steeper by 37bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 77% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (82bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.34 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 77%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed path chart anchors the current rally at Oct-2022. Month 48 stands at 251.2 vs 100, slightly ahead of the post-1990 dot-com path at the same age (235.7). That path went on to peak at month 113, while the 1994-anchored path peaked at month 69. On calendar alone, history does not say 'top now'. What is missing is the classic 2000 combination of euphoric retail sentiment plus a rate shock that breaks the leaders. Today one half is present (5.34% 10Y, a hiking Fed) and the other is absent (AAII bull–bear at -11.9). The mega-IPO pipeline (Anthropic reportedly targeting an October Nasdaq listing at speculative valuations) is the froth tell to watch (ipo_froth_pct and lt_eps_growth_pct are analyst estimates; lt_eps_growth_pct was not separately verified by search this run). Bottom line: this looks like an expensive, concentrated, complacent market rather than a 2000-style mania, and the vulnerability is rates more than retail euphoria.

⚔️Iran War

GlobalSecurity's Day 220 update (Oct 5) reports intense fighting around the Bab el-Mandeb. More than 270 combatants were killed in 24 hours; the Houthis struck Saudi airports and the Rabigh refinery, and Saudi Arabia conducted its first naval bombardment of Houthi ports. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey activated the 'Mecca Defence Alliance'. The same update notes Brent briefly fell below $100 on Oct 6, and that no Iranian attack on a host state or coalition strike ashore was reported. CBS reports the Houthis deny losing ground on the Red Sea coast and claim heavy Saudi casualties, and that oil eased despite the fighting. On diplomacy, President Trump said the war is 'essentially almost over' and the US is 'open' to talks while rejecting Tehran's Hormuz conditions (GlobalSecurity). Iran International reported Oct 3 that President Pezeshkian ruled out US talks as a third tanker in two days was hit near Hormuz. Iran's army spokesman has warned of possible preemptive strikes. Market read (analyst): the shipping-lane risk premium holds Brent at 101.48 pre-market, and talk of talks caps but does not remove it.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at 3.75–4.00% at the next meeting is the most likely outcome (inference). The September 16 FOMC hiked 25bp. On Oct 2, Warsh's deputies Jefferson and Williams publicly 'tempered rate hike bets' by stressing patience. The hawkish tail remains: Warsh has said stubborn inflation may require hikes.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his record: policy stays restrictive, with possibly one more hike if core PCE stays near 3%. Cuts would only come once PCE moves convincingly toward the 2% 'firm, fixed target' he set at Jackson Hole. Expect less forward guidance ('quieter' Fed) and, consistent with his long-held views, a preference for a smaller balance sheet. That last point is flagged as inference and was not reconfirmed in this run's sources.

At Jackson Hole (Aug 28) Warsh called inflation too high and July PCE at 3.7% 'concerning'. He named 2% PCE the 'firm, fixed target' and signaled hikes may be needed, a clearer signal than before (CNBC, PBS, Fed). He also advocated a 'quieter' central bank that avoids telegraphing moves. The FOMC then hiked to 3¾–4% on Sept 16 (Fed press conference transcript). Bloomberg reports that with Warsh refusing to guide, his top deputies stepped in Oct 2 to signal patience, and markets listened.
